title: Atrahasis, Standard Babylonian Tablet III
source: British Museum tablet photographs + eBL manuscript transliterations (eBL corpus edition L I.1, Story of the Flood (Atrahasis) (ed. E. Jiménez and G. Rozzi), SB III) + English of the eBL edition (B. R. Foster (eBL edition))
description: Atrahasis, Standard Babylonian Tablet III: 54 of 60 lines, each shown on a photographed cuneiform tablet (1 tablets), with the eBL transliteration of that tablet and B. R. Foster's English translation.
introduction:
The later version of the Flood episode.

Atrahasis ('Exceedingly Wise') is the Babylonian story of humanity from its creation to the Flood. The lesser gods rebel against their labour; humankind is created from clay and the flesh and blood of a slain god to do the work instead; when people multiply and their noise disturbs Enlil, he sends plague, drought and famine, and finally the Flood, which Atrahasis survives in a boat on the advice of Enki (Ea). The oldest near-complete copy was written at Sippar by the scribe Ipiq-Aya in the 17th century BCE. This page follows the line numbering of the electronic Babylonian Library edition.

How this page is built. Each section is a run of consecutive lines as written on one photographed clay tablet. For every line the eBL edition (https://www.ebl.lmu.de/corpus/L/1/1/SB/III) lists the manuscripts that carry it, with each tablet's own column and line numbers; the tablet chosen for each run is the photographed copy of the work with the most signs preserved there. Commentaries and texts that only quote a line are never chosen. School and excerpt tablets are used only for lines that no photographed library copy preserves as well, and only where they carry the line as text; their sections say so. The original text is eBL's transliteration of that tablet's signs (not a modern composite text): square brackets mark broken signs, x an illegible sign, # a damaged sign, ? an uncertain reading, and words in {braces} are determinatives; the notes give a key to every sign used on this page, and eBL's layout codes are written out in words (for example '(line break)' or '(blank space)'). Superscript numbers are the line numbers of the eBL edition, used in both the Akkadian and the English. The English is B. R. Foster's translation in the eBL edition (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0), one line of English per line of the text; italics mark uncertain renderings, as in the source. Where the tablet is broken, the English still translates the whole line of eBL's composite text; each section's note names the lines that are broken on its tablet.

Finding a line on the photograph. Each section names the tablet, the face and column, and the tablet's own line numbers (a prime, as in 5', counts from the first preserved line of a broken column). On a tablet with six columns the obverse carries columns i-iii from left to right; the reverse, turned over from bottom to top, carries columns iv-vi from right to left. The photographs often show the obverse above the reverse with the edges around them; a fragment preserves only part of this layout.

This page shows 54 of the 60 lines of the eBL edition (90%), from 1 tablet in the British Museum: K.4539 (Nineveh).

Lines not shown. 6 of the 60 lines of the eBL edition are not shown, because no photographed copy of the work used here carries them: 1 (no photograph in eBL: Ist-B.116 (Istanbul Archaeological Museum); not in the eBL Fragmentarium (no photograph there): IM.124649); 2 (no photograph in eBL: Ist-B.116 (Istanbul Archaeological Museum)); 66-68 (no manuscript preserves it); 132 (no manuscript preserves it). A line is shown only on a photographed tablet that carries it as text. Commentaries and other texts that quote a line (letters, rituals, god lists) are not used as witnesses, because they carry it with explanations or inside another text; tablets without a photograph in eBL are not used, because the line could not be shown on its tablet.
translator_notes: Akkadian: eBL transliteration of the signs on the photographed tablet (manuscript-level ATF), not a composite text.
English: B. R. Foster's translation in the eBL edition; it renders eBL's composite text, including restorations from other tablets.
Line numbers: eBL edition. Each section also gives the tablet's own column and line numbers.

Signs in the Akkadian: [ ] broken away; x illegible sign; # damaged sign; ? uncertain reading; ! sign corrected by the editor; ... broken signs of unknown number; ( ) signs perhaps broken away; { } determinative.

translation.text:
3[I have imposed] your [… forced labor] on man.
4[From] this day onwards I will set the gods free!
5“[You have bestowed] clamor upon humankind.
6“I have imposed [the drudgery] of god on man.
7[…] … for mankind
8“[You have] slaughtered [the god], along with his inspiration.”
9Thus was the speech [of Mama].
10[The gods ran together] and kissed her feet, (saying,)
11[‘Formerly] we used to call you [Ma]mi,
12Now let your name be Mistress-of-All-the-Gods
13[They enter]ed the house of destiny
14Did prince Ea (and) wise Mami.
15With the birth-goddesses assembled
16He trod the clay in her presence.
17She kept reciting the incantation,
18Ea, seated before her, was prompting her.
19After she had finished her incantation,
20She nipped off fourteen pieces of clay.
21Seven she put on the right,
translation.scan_note: British Museum K.4539: obverse, column ii, the tablet's own lines 1' to 19'. eBL's corpus edition (https://www.ebl.lmu.de/corpus/L/1/1/SB/III) attributes SB III 3-21 to this manuscript at these column and line numbers. Photograph checked: one face only, a fragment about 3.5 cm wide with about 9 lines; no legible ink number. Alone it cannot carry eBL's 54 lines (obverse column ii 37, reverse column iii 17), but with the three linked pieces (K.5902, K.7816+K.13863, K.17752) the set shows about 45 to 50 lines on both faces. eBL treats K.4539 + K.5902 + K.7816 + K.17752 as one manuscript and holds a separate photograph of each of these pieces; it does not say which piece carries which line, so the photographs of K.4539 + K.5902 + K.7816 + K.17752 are linked, and the lines are on one or more of them. On this tablet of line 3 only illegible traces (x) survive and lines 4-21 are partly broken (square brackets and x in the Akkadian). The English of these lines translates eBL's composite text, so it includes words that are not preserved on this tablet but are restored from other manuscripts or by the editors. Square brackets in the English mark eBL's restorations in its composite text; words that survive on other tablets carry no brackets even where this tablet is broken.
